findings.claim: 'that is site knowledge earning Level 4, not scene-setting'.
findings.truth: 'Level 4' is a banned band name and would fail the whole unit at validation. Replaced with 'top-band site knowledge'.
findings.evidence: checker brief, banned-strings list

findings.claim: 'The chronicler Walter of Guisborough recorded the king's personal motto: ‘Keep faith’.'
findings.truth: The motto (Pactum Serva) is not recorded by Walter of Guisborough in any source I could verify; it is known from the tomb at Westminster Abbey, which lesson 11 itself teaches is a later addition. Attribution removed, motto kept.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Edward I of England' - no mention of the motto or of Guisborough recording it

findings.claim: 'Westminster II also confirmed something with much wider effects: the Statute of Winchester, also issued in 1285'.
findings.truth: Westminster II (Easter parliament 1285) and Winchester (October 1285) were separate statutes; Westminster II did not confirm Winchester. Lesson 5 already dates Winchester correctly to October 1285.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with lesson 5; standard chronology of the 1285 statutes

findings.claim: 'Balliol (founded by John de Balliol's widow Dervorguilla in the 1260s, statutes 1282)'.
findings.truth: John de Balliol founded the college about 1263 and died in 1268; his widow Dervorguilla provided the endowment and wrote the statutes in 1282. She was not his widow in the 1260s.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Balliol College, Oxford'

findings.claim: 'It required Jews from age twelve to wear a larger yellow felt badge in the shape of the Tablets of the Law.'
findings.truth: The 1275 Statute of the Jewry required the badge from the age of seven; the three pence poll tax applied from the age of twelve. The lesson conflates the two ages.
findings.evidence: terms of the Statute of the Jewry 1275 (badge from age seven, tax from age twelve)

findings.claim: 'not formally repealed until 1656'; knowledge check 4 asks when Jews were 'formally readmitted'.
findings.truth: The Edict of Expulsion was never formally repealed. After the Whitehall Conference of 1655-56 Cromwell allowed Jews to return in practice; there was no formal readmission.
findings.evidence: standard account of the 1656 readmission (de facto, no repeal of the 1290 edict)

findings.claim: 'blood libel' defined as '...; sometimes called the ‘blood libel’.'
findings.truth: Circular definition. Replaced with 'also called a ritual murder charge'.
findings.evidence: glossary self-reference

findings.claim: 'franchise' defined as '...; sometimes called a franchise.'
findings.truth: Circular definition. Replaced with 'sometimes called a liberty'.
findings.evidence: glossary self-reference

findings.claim: 'concentric walls (an outer ring inside an inner ring)', repeated in a mark scheme as 'an outer wall inside an inner wall'.
findings.truth: Concentric design is the reverse: a lower outer wall rings a higher inner wall. As written the description is inside out.
findings.evidence: definition of concentric castle design

findings.claim: 'He performed homage to Edward at Westminster in 1278.'
findings.truth: Llywelyn did homage after the Treaty of Aberconwy at Christmas 1277; 1278 is the year of his marriage to Eleanor de Montfort at Worcester (13 October 1278). Corrected in the content and in the mark scheme that repeats it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Llywelyn ap Gruffudd' - homage at Christmas 1277; marriage 13 October 1278

findings.claim: 'In July 1295 they appointed a council of twelve to govern in Balliol's name and signed the auld alliance with Philip IV of France'.
findings.truth: The council of twelve dates from July 1295; the treaty with France was sealed in Paris in October 1295. The sentence dates both to July.
findings.evidence: chronology of the 1295 Franco-Scottish treaty

findings.claim: Balliol's 'reign lasted barely three years'.
findings.truth: He was inaugurated on 30 November 1292 and stripped of his regalia on 8 July 1296 - three years and seven months.
findings.evidence: dates given in the same lesson

findings.claim: 'Returned to Scotland in 1996; on display at Edinburgh Castle.'
findings.truth: The Stone of Scone left Edinburgh Castle and has been on permanent display at Perth Museum since it opened on 30 March 2024.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Stone of Scone'

findings.claim: 'In May 1307 Bruce returned to Ayrshire and won small but symbolic engagements at Glentrool and Loudoun Hill.'
findings.truth: Bruce returned to Carrick in February 1307; Glen Trool was fought in April and Loudoun Hill on 10 May 1307.
findings.evidence: chronology of Bruce's 1307 campaign

findings.claim: 'Four pivotal battles shaped the First War of Scottish Independence' - the list includes 'the campaign of 1303-04 ending in Edward's acceptance of Scottish surrender at Strathord'.
findings.truth: Strathord was a negotiated surrender, not a battle. Relabelled 'four turning points' in the key fact and the revision tip.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own wording

findings.claim: 'longbowmen' defined as 'The long English bow drawn to the ear, capable of launching armour-piercing arrows over 200 metres'.
findings.truth: The entry defines a bow, not the bowmen, and the armour-piercing range claim is contested. Rewritten to describe the archers.
findings.evidence: term/definition mismatch

findings.claim: 'a young knight from Renfrewshire called William Wallace' (spring 1297).
findings.truth: The same lesson says Wallace was knighted in March 1298. He was not a knight when the rising began.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction in the lesson

findings.claim: 'the house was abandoned by the early fifteenth century and has long stood a roofless shell'.
findings.truth: The house was still standing later than that; it had been mostly demolished by the time it passed to the Smythe family in the mid-seventeenth century.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Acton Burnell Castle'

findings.claim: 'Edward I spent thirty-five years at war'.
findings.truth: Thirty-five years is the length of the reign (1272-1307), not of continuous war.
findings.evidence: regnal dates

findings.claim: 'But look closer, as the examiner wants you to.'
findings.truth: Invented exam claim inside the article text. Removed.
findings.evidence: checker brief - invented exam claims

findings.claim: Lesson descriptions run to 102 (lesson 9), 125 (lesson 12) and 130 (lesson 13) characters.
findings.truth: The validator caps a lesson description at under 100 characters. All three shortened; lesson 9 is now 95, lesson 12 is 93, lesson 13 is 87.
findings.evidence: checker brief - validator limits

findings.claim: 'The Statute of the Jewry, mounting persecution and Edward's edict expelling England's.'
findings.truth: The description is cut off mid-phrase; the noun is missing. Now ends 'expelling England's Jews'.
findings.evidence: the field itself

findings.claim: Twenty-one flashcards answer with a bare year or a single word ('1285.', '1290.', 'Mining.', 'Sapping.', 'Thirteen.', 'Robert Burnell.'), and seven answer with a comma list ('Grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy.'; 'Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and Beaumaris.'; 'Heavy cavalry, mass infantry, longbow archers and crossbowmen.').
findings.truth: List answers fail the validator and bare answers fail the substantive-question rule. Each list card was rewritten around one idea (question changed where the question itself demanded a list); each bare answer was given a few words of substance. No duplicate answers and no answer over 30 words after the edits.
findings.evidence: checker brief - flashcard rules

findings.claim: Every lesson from 1 to 11 carries a 16-mark judgement essay on depth-study content (for example 'The wool trade was the most important factor in shaping Edward I's government').
findings.truth: This section's only 16-mark question is always tied to the specified historic-environment site, so a 16-mark essay on the wool trade or the statutes will never be set. Two options. (a) Keep them as extended-writing practice with the stem corrected to the real judgement form - which is what these edits do, replacing the non-AQA stems 'Evaluate the claim that this is correct' and 'Argue, using examples...' with a statement plus 'How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.' (b) Re-anchor all eleven to the specified site - but the site changes annually, so every question would need rewriting each year. Recommend (a), and keep the site-anchored practice in lessons 12 and 13 where it belongs.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Section B question 4: 'Essay question linked to specified site'
findings.ruling: Keep the 16-mark essays as judgement practice with the corrected stem; not re-anchored to a yearly-changing site.

findings.claim: 'Edward employed Genoese and Gascon crossbowmen for siegework'.
findings.truth: Gascon crossbowmen in Edward I's service are well attested; Genoese crossbowmen are associated with French service at Crecy in 1346. I could not verify Genoese crossbowmen in Edward I's armies from the permitted sources, so I have left it rather than guess.
findings.evidence: not verifiable from Wikipedia/National Archives/Britannica within this session

findings.claim: 'his grandson's Statute of Treasons in 1352'.
findings.truth: Edward III was indeed Edward I's grandson. The statute is 25 Edward III, conventionally cited as the Treason Act 1351 although the parliament sat into 1352. Both datings are defensible, so left alone.
findings.evidence: regnal-year dating of 25 Edw. III

findings.claim: Lessons 12 and 13 name the Battle of Stirling Bridge as the 2027 specified site and Acton Burnell Castle as the 2028 specified site.
findings.truth: AQA publishes the specified site three years in advance on its own website. I could not check that list from the permitted sources. Tom should confirm both allocations against AQA's published schedule before the 2027 cohort starts, because the whole of both lessons hangs on it.
findings.evidence: spec: 'For all series the specified site will be published three years in advance at aqa.org.uk/history'

findings.claim: No lesson mentions SPaG marks on the 16-mark site question.
findings.truth: Correct as it stands, and worth recording because it is easy to get wrong: on this paper the four SPaG marks sit on the thematic study's 16-mark essay, not on the British depth study's site question. The depth section is a clean 40 marks over four questions. No edit needed.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2: Section A thematic question 4 totals 20 marks including SPaG; Section B totals 8+8+8+16 = 40

findings.claim: The unit contains no practice at the 8-mark interpretation question, which is the first question in this section.
findings.truth: A gap rather than an error, and one I have not filled: writing that practice needs interpretations, and any composed interpretation would have to be labelled as composed rather than presented as a real historian's words. Worth queueing as a build task.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Section B question 1 (AO4, 8 marks)

summary: All 13 lessons taught question forms this paper does not set - 25 four-mark 'Describe two features', 20 'Explain the significance of' and 18 'Explain the effects of' - so every practice question except two narrative accounts and the two site essays was in the wrong form; all were converted to the real 8-mark 'Explain what was important about' and 'Write an account of' questions with retariffed mark schemes, and the non-AQA 16-mark stems were rewritten as judgement essays. One banned band name ('Level 4') in lesson 12 would have failed the whole unit. Twenty-two substantive errors of fact or definition were fixed, including Balliol College's founder, Llywelyn's homage of Christmas 1277, concentric castle walls described inside out, the age at which the 1275 badge applied, the never-repealed 1290 edict, the auld alliance dated to July instead of October 1295, and the Stone of Scone, which left Edinburgh Castle for Perth Museum in 2024.
